passage: "Your Uncle Suresh does it too," Manjula told Shreya, pointing at her granddaughter's hand. "Nodding at me with his eyes on that phone. I used to think he was listening because his head kept bobbing." She tucked a cushion behind her back. "One day I was telling him about my knee doctor's appointment, and he said, 'Mm-hm, sure,' and then asked me to repeat everything. I wasn't cross. It was only that I couldn't tell from the nodding." Shreya set down her phone. "What did you do?" "I asked him one small question: 'Can you tell me what I said last?' We both laughed, and after that he put the phone face down when I began."

qa.q: What was Manjula telling Uncle Suresh about?
qa.a: She was telling him about her knee doctor's appointment.

qa.q: What does Suresh's nodding show about his attention, and how did he feel when caught out?
qa.a: It doesn't prove he was listening: his head bobbed while his eyes stayed on the phone, so he was probably half-listening. When Manjula asked what she had said last, he laughed along, amused rather than defensive.

qa.q: What could Shreya try if she isn't sure someone is listening to her?
qa.a: She could ask a brief question such as 'What did I say last?' to check gently, instead of assuming.

qa.q: How might Manjula have felt when Suresh asked her to repeat everything?
qa.a: She may have felt a little unheard, though she says she wasn't cross, and she chose a light question rather than a complaint.

grounding: A teen nodding while looking at a phone may or may not be listening, and a brief question checks it.

passage: The metro platform was loud with announcements and rush-hour footsteps, and Vidya had to raise her voice to be heard. She was telling Raghav about her audition, one of the most important things in her month. Raghav nodded along, murmuring "yeah, yeah," but his eyes kept dropping to his phone in his hand. Vidya couldn't tell whether he was really with her or waiting for a message. She wasn't sure the noise had let her words through at all. She stopped mid-sentence and said, "Sorry, it's so loud. Did you catch that last part, or should I pause?" Raghav looked up, startled. "Honestly, I'm waiting for my cab to be confirmed. Tell me again, I'm listening now."

qa.q: Where were Vidya and Raghav standing?
qa.a: They were on the metro platform.

qa.q: What was Vidya worried about as Raghav nodded?
qa.a: She wasn't sure whether he was really with her or waiting for a message, since nodding and glancing at a phone don't show attention on their own.

qa.q: What did Vidya do that helped clear things up?
qa.a: She asked a brief, friendly question, checking if he had caught the last part, instead of guessing or getting annoyed.

qa.q: How might Raghav have felt when Vidya stopped mid-sentence?
qa.a: He was probably startled and a little caught out, but honest, since he explained that he was waiting for his cab and asked her to repeat it.

grounding: A teen nodding while glancing at a phone may be listening or elsewhere, and a brief question checks attention.

passage:
In a café near their college in Pune, Vidya was telling Yusuf about her fight with her mother. Halfway through, he glanced at his phone. Then again. He nodded.
Vidya stopped. "Are you even listening?"
Yusuf looked up. "Yes! Your mum wants you to do the engineering entrance and you want to do design, and she said design isn't a real job, and you cried in the auto."
Vidya blinked. That was exactly it.
"Then why do you keep looking at your phone?"
"My bus. The last one is at seven, and the app keeps changing the time. Sorry. I should have said."
He turned the phone face down. "Go on. What did you say back to her?"
Vidya relaxed. She'd been sure he was elsewhere. His posture said one thing; his answer said another.
"I said I'd show her my portfolio."
"Good. Do that."

qa.q: When was Yusuf's last bus?
qa.a: The last one is at seven.

qa.q: What was Vidya feeling when Yusuf glanced at his phone?
qa.a: Vidya felt hurt and unheard, sure he wasn't listening to something important.

qa.q: What checked whether Yusuf was really listening?
qa.a: Vidya's brief question, "Are you even listening?", which showed he had heard every detail despite looking at his phone.

qa.q: How did Yusuf see his phone glances?
qa.a: He saw them as checking the bus time, not as ignoring Vidya, though he realised he should have said so.

grounding: The scene shows a teenager nodding while glancing at a phone, and a brief question revealing he was actually listening.

passage:
"So the model will have three layers, and the water flows through the sand first, then the charcoal, then—"
Arohi stopped. Wasim was staring out of the classroom window.
"Wasim."
"Hmm?"
"What did I just say?"
Wasim turned red. "Something about... layers?"
"And?"
"Honestly? I missed it. Sorry."
Arohi folded her arms. "You nodded the whole time."
"I know. I was thinking about my cricket trial. It's at four." He rubbed his face. "Nodding is what I do when I'm lost in my head."
"That's annoying."
"I know. Can you say it again? I'm here now."
She explained again. This time he asked, "Why charcoal after sand?"
"Because sand catches the big bits first."
"Okay. I'll make the charcoal layer."
Arohi smiled. "Now you're listening."
"Now I'm listening," he agreed.

qa.q: What time was Wasim's cricket trial?
qa.a: It's at four.

qa.q: What was Arohi feeling when Wasim couldn't repeat what she said?
qa.a: Arohi felt annoyed and a little hurt, since his nodding had made her think he was listening.

qa.q: What did Arohi's question achieve?
qa.a: It showed that Wasim's nodding did not mean attention, and gave him a chance to admit it and really listen.

qa.q: How might Wasim have felt when Arohi asked "What did I just say?"
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and caught out, turning red, but honest enough to admit he'd been distracted.

grounding: The dialogue shows nodding while looking elsewhere hiding distraction, and a brief question checking attention.

passage:
Last Sunday my father, Nitin, sat down next to me on the sofa and started talking about summer courses. Coding camp, art camp, maybe a language. I nodded along. I said "mm" a lot. I was scrolling through photos of my friend's party on my phone.
After a while he stopped and said, calmly, "Kalyani, which one did you like?"
I looked up. I had no idea what he'd said. My face went hot.
"Sorry, Papa. I wasn't listening."
He didn't get angry. He said, "You were nodding. I thought you were."
That stuck with me. My nodding had fooled both of us.
I put the phone in the other room, and we went through the list again. I actually liked the language course.
Now when I notice myself nodding on autopilot, I ask myself what the person just said. If I can't answer, I put the phone away.

qa.q: What was Kalyani scrolling through?
qa.a: Photos of a friend's party.

qa.q: What was Kalyani feeling when she couldn't answer Papa's question?
qa.a: Kalyani felt embarrassed and a little guilty, her face going hot, realising the nodding had hidden a lack of listening.

qa.q: What small habit did Kalyani take from this?
qa.a: Checking silently what the person just said when nodding on autopilot, and putting the phone away if no answer comes.

qa.q: How did Nitin read Kalyani's nodding?
qa.a: He took the nodding as a sign of listening, until a brief question showed it wasn't.

grounding: The account shows nodding while glancing at a phone hiding distraction, and a brief question checking attention.

passage:
Tutor's note, Saturday batch
While I explained the trigonometry identities, Eshaan sat sideways, nodding, eyes flicking to the phone under his desk every half minute. Himani sat straight, pen ready, looking right at me. I was sure I knew which of them was listening. Rather than take the phone, I asked each of them one quick question. Eshaan answered his perfectly and added, a bit sheepishly, that he was watching for a message because his mother was at the hospital for his sister's scan and had promised to text. Himani went pink and admitted she had followed the first part but lost track and was too embarrassed to say. So both my guesses were wrong. I told Eshaan he could keep the phone face up on the desk today, and after class I went over the second half with Himani. From next week I'll do a two-question check halfway through, for everyone.

qa.q: Why was Eshaan watching his phone?
qa.a: His mother was at the hospital for his sister's scan and had promised to text.

qa.q: What was Himani feeling when she went pink?
qa.a: Himani felt embarrassed at having lost track after the first part, which her attentive posture had hidden; there may also have been relief at getting help after class.

qa.q: What did the tutor learn, and what will change?
qa.a: The tutor learned that posture didn't show who was listening, and will add a quick two-question check halfway through for everyone instead of guessing.

qa.q: What would have changed if the tutor had taken Eshaan's phone?
qa.a: Eshaan might have missed news about his sister's scan and felt unfairly punished, even though he was actually following.

grounding: It shows a teenager who looks distracted actually listening and one who looks attentive being lost, and a brief question checking attention better than posture.
